item.title: Rip out ugly clutter to help revive UK high streets, says thinktank
item.description: Exclusive: Report says restricting cars and freeing up pavement space could be a cheap way to entice shoppers The long decline of the high street is a problem that has gripped British governments for years. But what if there was a solution no one had considered before – doing it all on the cheap? Spending less money is, admittedly, just one element of a report led by the urban thinktank Create Streets. But it does argue that rather than multimillion-pound revamps, a better answer could be smaller changes aimed at making town and city centres more appealing. Continue reading...

item.title: Flights stopped across US due to ‘extraordinary circumstances’, FAA says
item.description: The US Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide on Friday afternoon. The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety”. However, the government didn’t provide any details about the reason. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that, the last time had been after the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks.

item.description: Rescue efforts under way as American Heritage takes on water; governor confirms incident in Mississippi River Tanker collides with cruise ship on Mississippi River in New Orleans A video circulating around social media shows a different angle during the moment the ship was falling on its side into the water. Passengers can be seen climbing onto the balconies’ railing to avoid sliding into the river as the ship turned horizontally. Several uniformed people can be seen running away from the scene, likely to gather equipment that would help rescue efforts. Martin J Davies, a maritime expert at Tulane University, told local news outlet Fox 8 that he suspected the incident was caused by either steerage failure or engine failure. Continue reading...

Spain won 1-0 at the Bernabéu but the occasion was ruined by racist abuse directed at England’s black players from the stands. England have since played three games in Spain, although they refused to return to Madrid for the first of them in 2009. The match was moved to Seville. There were no ­problems in any of the three; the second was in Alicante in 2015, the third back in Seville in 2018. Continue reading...

item.title: ‘No one is unbeatable’: Tuchel eager for England to impose style on Spain
item.description: Manager calls Sunday’s Nations League decider a ‘final’ as preparations for Euro 2028 ratchet up a level Proof of concept. It is Thomas Tuchel’s latest buzz phrase. The England manager has dropped it into the conversation pretty regularly since the Friday of last week when he named his squad for this international window, the one that was always going to decide whether his team finished first or second in their Nations League group. By it, Tuchel means a test of his methods, what he is trying to build – or, more accurately, fine-tune – as he turns his gaze towards Euro 2028 and tries to move on from the devastation of the World Cup semi-final exit against Argentina . The test does not come any bigger than the one which faces him and his players in Madrid on Sunday night. Continue reading...

item.description: The ‘first lady’ of Hobart’s Museum of Old and New Art has launched an OnlyFans portal with an ambitious – and controversial – goal The forestry workers took unusual care as they picked their way through the mossy undergrowth of a Tasmanian forest. They were carrying a small group of furries – humans in animal suits that can cost thousands of dollars – mindful of not letting any tails drag in the mud. Hired as production crew for the day, they were more used to hearing the drone of heavy logging machinery than the moans of animal lust. Once the furries were in place, the director closed the set so that they could film their group sex scene in private. “They were just adorable. Even when they’re doing adult acts, it still just looks really cute and kind of innocuous,” artist Kirsha Kaechele says. Continue reading...

item.title: The Guardian view on press freedom: authoritarians target journalism because it matters | Editorial
item.description: From Cairo to Moscow to Washington, governments are turning up the pressure on media workers Lina Attalah is an influential Egyptian journalist. Yet until last month, even she was unaware of a major and concerning piece of news: her own conviction. In 2024, a court issued her a one-year sentence for “spreading false news” and running a website without a licence – which she had repeatedly sought to obtain – after trying her in absentia, even though she was in the country. Ms Attalah learned of the case only after she was separately tried in October , resulting in a large fine and an order for the closure of the Mada Masr website. She faces retrial later this month. Meanwhile, the entire newsroom of the fact-checking website Matsadash remain in detention weeks after authorities snatched the six journalists on charges including joining and financing a terrorist group and spreading false news. Their lawyers say that they have been tortured and forced to record fabricated confessions. Conti

item.title: The Guardian view on M John Harrison’s Booker win: a new frontier for science fiction | Editorial
item.description: The End of Everything is a novel for our age of permacrisis. Genre boundaries belong to the past “Science fiction will never be Literature with a capital ‘L,’” began a New York Times review of Margaret Atwood’s novel Oryx and Crake back in 2003. Now, the seemingly impossible has happened – M John Harrison’s The End of Everything is the first science fiction novel to win the Booker prize. Fans have hailed this as a victory for a long-marginalised genre. The author himself was not so sure. “Writing science fiction is the last thing I want to do,” he said with characteristic iconoclasm at an event before the prize. The sci-fi v literary or “mainstream” fiction debate is as endless and battle-strewn as a fantasy saga. The late Ursula K Le Guin, a giant of the form, famously took Atwood to task for her reluctance to use the term science fiction for some of her novels, including Oryx and Crake: “She doesn’t want the literary bigots to shove her into the literary ghetto.” Harrison doesn’t wan

item.title: Don’t just blame the culture for keeping powerful men’s dirty secrets. Blame the law too | Gaby Hinsliff
item.description: It is important to understand just how effectively perpetrators of abuse have used lawyers as their shields. A challenge to that can’t come soon enough There will be empty shelves in many bedrooms this weekend, where the David Walliams books once stood. For parents of a certain era, there was no escaping that particular publishing-industrial complex, and I certainly did my share of wearily reading Gangsta Granny or Mr Stink on repeat. At his peak, Walliams was the bestselling children’s author in Britain for 100 weeks straight, to say nothing of the spin-off theatre productions, Christmas specials, countless World Book Day costumes, and that family-friendly stint as a judge on Britain’s Got Talent during which we now learn he was reportedly inviting teenagers to his dressing room . “What I try and do most of all in my books is encourage reluctant readers,” he told breakfast TV’s Lorraine Kelly in 2024, the year before publisher HarperCollins finally dropped him after allegations over h

item.title: McGree helps Socceroos put drama behind them and leave Qatar reeling
item.description: Qatar 0-3 Australia (McGree 5, Yengi 32, Irankunda 40) Julen Lopetegui under pressure as Qatar head coach It was a win almost as comfortable as the buildup had been turbulent, as the Socceroos placed the drama of a week dominated by talk of everything but the football aside and cruised to a comprehensive 3-0 win over Qatar. Pressing high, Australia’s men were ruthless in attack and dominant whenever their opponents even thought about getting forward, putting the result beyond doubt inside the opening 45 minutes . It took until the 38th for Qatar to register a touch in the Australia penalty area, and by that point they were down 2-0, with the third added for good measure just two minutes later. When Almoez Ali registered the reigning Asian champions’ first shot in the 72nd minute, Tony Popovic had emptied his bench, and the debutant Sam Klein hurled himself in front of the attempt before Patrick Beach had to worry about making a save. item.title: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both | Jonathan Freedland
item.description: The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world For politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices. Andy Burnham is a prime example. item.title: Why Chelsea and Manchester City’s WSL clash is not as season-defining as you think
item.description: Neither side have lost in the league yet but a more competitive division should take title race to the wire There was a time when the games between the top three – traditionally Chelsea, Manchester City and Arsenal – were title-deciders. Where every point taken off a title rival was key. Such was the gap in investment and quality between those teams and the rest of the Women’s Super League, it was extremely rare that points would be dropped to teams outside that elite clique. As the WSL has grown in investment, profile and size, that narrative has started to shift a little. The investment gap is still large from the top to the bottom of the league. But increased investment among the best of the rest and even among those teams further down the table, as well as an increase in high-quality coaches with the tactical and technical vision to get more from players, is having an impact. item.description: Heavy rain and strong winds have also caused disruption across British Columbia, Canada, over the last week Storm Charles has brought destructive weather to the Iberian peninsula this week, particularly in Portugal and the far south of Spain. Heavy rain and strong south-westerly winds arrived first in the Portuguese island of Madeira, before the system headed towards the mainland on 11 November. A wind gust of 84.5mph (136 km/h) was recorded at Funchal airport, alongside rainfall totals reaching 355mm (13.97in) in 12 hours. In Lisbon, 183 flights were cancelled on Wednesday, about a third of its normal daily traffic, while Madrid Barajas airport had 155 cancellations. After causing widespread flooding in Spain and Portugal, the system moved on a north-easterly track through southern France and then towards northern Italy. But although she’s a dab hand at graceful, timeless presentation (and has a truly remarkable voice) Aalegra’s music has often struggled to match up to its aesthetic, hampered by her love of the greats and a penchant for broadly generic lyrics. Her most recent album, 2021’s Temporary Highs in the Violet Skies , made some headway toward carving out a more distinctive sound, thanks to sparky and inventive production from Tyler, the Creator, No ID, P2J and the Neptunes, but still didn’t quite feel like the right fit. item.title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John
item.description: Football and the art world have long remained distant but the breadth of entries for this year’s award reveals a healthy revival It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player . You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball. These, in any case, were exceptions. But even the promise of some very bad weather was not enough to deter housing protesters from setting up camp for another night on the streets. item.title: The sinister power of Friday 13th: how this maligned date affects our lives
item.description: Property sales that complete on this day have a lower median price. Air fares are cheaper. Weddings are non-existent. And motor collisions increase. How did it become so mired in superstition? “I have only worked one Friday 13th wedding in my 14 years in business,” says Caroline Smyth, a photographer and celebrant based in Larne, Northern Ireland. “I definitely think it is down to the fact that it’s a date surrounded by superstition. People are maybe afraid it’s a bad omen for their marriage.” Smyth’s sole Friday 13th wedding, in September 2013, was the first she ever photographed – and it kickstarted her career. But for many businesses, the date is not so auspicious. From weddings to flights, job interviews to elective surgeries, many people avoid booking anything of significance on this date, believing it to be bad luck. Continue reading...

item.title: Cunk on Cinema review – Diane Morgan baffles Hollywood with some of the stupidest jokes ever told
item.description: This sensationally idiotic guide to film history is hilarious. From a crude Mary Poppins gag to confusing the hell out of Michael Bay, I could listen to Cunk’s surreal tosh all day In a world of slow-burn, jargon-littered dramas, there’s something to be said for the TV programme that sets out its stall within the first 12 seconds. Cunk on Cinema is one such programme. The latest series from Diane Morgan’s sensationally idiotic documentarian is a three-part history of film that begins with our host reeling off some of humanity’s greatest achievements in her deadpan Bolton tones. Specifically, “conquering the landscape, growing the great wall of Chinese, discovering Mona Lisa and inventing global warming”. If you think that list is funny, you’ll enjoy what is essentially a vehicle for some of the stupidest jokes ever written. If you find that kind of malapropism and misapprehension childish, I suggest you switch off immediately. We first encountered Philomena Cunk in 2012 as a spoof talk

item.title: I’ve had a stinking cold this week – and I’m longing for good advice | Adrian Chiles
item.description: Heavy and light colds tend to pass more quickly than middle-of-the-road ones. But should I stay in bed or continue mixing with others? How to define the cold that’s ruining your day? There’s a hierarchy. We start with the sniffle, the mere runny nose, scratchy throat or just feeling a little off. This is the slight cold. The nose becoming more blocked than runny, and a cough coming into play, entitles you to call it a heavy cold. Any of the aforementioned symptoms worsening, accompanied by hotness, shiveriness, aching and general misery, gives you the right to call it a stinking cold. There’s also a malady known as man-flu, but I have no truck with such a lazy, gender-specific categorisation. The only good thing about the stinking cold is that you have the green light to do sod all and repair to bed. This was me for three days this week, and it has firmed up a theory I have long held that you’re better off getting a stinker because it tends to come and go and be done with more quickly

item.title: Ex-member of radical Marxist group scales balcony, escapes house arrest in Argentina
item.description: Leonardo Bertulazzi, 74, awaiting extradition to Italy, reportedly used harness to flee custody A 74-year-old former member of Italy ’s radical Marxist group the Red Brigades has escaped from house arrest in Argentina , the country’s security ministry confirmed on Wednesday, after he reportedly hid his ankle monitor inside a tube of pork and lowered himself from a fifth-floor balcony. Authorities placed Leonardo Bertulazzi under house arrest in Buenos Aires in 2024, prior to his extradition to Italy to serve a 27-year prison sentence. item.title: Does M John Harrison’s Booker win mean science fiction is finally accepted by a ‘snobby’ literary establishment?
item.description: Kazuo Ishiguro, Jeff VanderMeer, Olivia Laing and other writers weigh in on the publishing world’s genre wars As M John Harrison was announced as the Booker prize winner on Monday evening, the 81-year-old looked gobsmacked. Decades into his career, and long overlooked by the mainstream literary establishment, he had just won a prize that has never before rewarded a writer known for science fiction, with a decidedly fantastical book. His fans, many leading authors among them, are thrilled. “For decades it was a standard – and correct – nerd whine to point out that sentence for sentence, book for book, Harrison was one of the greatest writers out there, full stop, but that ‘mainstream’ prizes never reflected that,” says China Miéville, who last week won the Goldsmiths prize with his 1,200-page speculative novel The Rouse . Sometimes they are electrifying and sometimes they are deathly dull. Sometimes they are completely baffling. My absolute favourite kind of show is the one that makes me want to run home and change my outfit. A show that makes me think: there it is! That’s exactly what I want to wear. The show was 63 different skirts – some with a sweater, some with a bra top, some with a jacket, but the point was the skirts. item.title: Touch of evil: the terrifying truth about sleep paralysis
item.description: One in five people have experienced this frightening state – and the Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal has dedicated his career to studying it. Could it be a portal to a deeper understanding of the mind? The Harvard neuroscientist Baland Jalal is considering the unfathomable depths of the human brain. “It can contemplate itself, and vast galaxies, spirits, souls, poetry, Einstein. Yet you hold it in your hand and it seems so trivial.” Jalal’s passion – the subject that drove him to become a scientist – is sleep paralysis, a brain glitch that can fill its host with terror so palpable that it can cause lasting trauma. “What you get very close to in sleep paralysis,” he says, “is that subjective world of the mind. It’s very hard to put into words.” He should know – he’s spent 271 pages trying to do so. His new book, The Phantom Mind, argues that by exploring the borderlands of sleep, where sleep paralysis occurs, we can delve deeper into how all aspects of our minds work. He may wear a

item.title: Is No 10 still the best, or No 41? The myths and maths of Premier League shirt numbers
item.description: While No 9s still score the most goals and No 1s try to stop them, trends have changed since the introduction of squad numbers in the early 1990s How much is a shirt number worth? It costs £8 if you want two digits added to the back of Arsenal’s 2026-27 home shirt, whereas Manchester City add on £16 for customisation, whether you want a name as well as a number or not. That is cheap compared to what baseball players decide among themselves. Juan Soto bought Brett Baty a $92,000 (£69,000) car in exchange for getting his preferred number (22) when he joined the New York Mets last year. But that’s baseball, where they allow players to wear ‘0’. Anything goes. Continue reading...

item.description: AI provider keys that customers stored on Railway were stolen in an October breach and used to commit an estimated $740,000 in unauthorized spending, the platform-as-a-service provider said yesterday. item.title: Canadian Authorities Kill 4 Bears Involved in Deadly Attack on Hikers
item.description: Wildlife authorities said evidence, including animal DNA, conclusively linked a sow and her three cubs to the deaths of two women along a hiking trail in British Columbia.

item.title: Microsoft Researchers Show AI Agents Can Be Backdoored by Editing Fewer Than 10 Neurons
item.description: An AI model can be given a hidden backdoor by editing fewer than 10 of its rarely used neurons, without retraining the model, Microsoft researchers have shown. When a chosen trigger appears, the model outputs an attacker's command, which an agent using that model would run with the agent's own permissions. The attacker must be able to change the model's weights. The team tested the method on

item.description: BBC Sport charts Jarma Mohamed's surprising football journey from Premier League academies to the Somalia national team, via an app and Jersey Bulls.

item.title: DW Science explainer on the default mode network: what your brain does when you aren't focusing on anything, and why it's important.
item.description: Doing nothing might be the ultimate brain hack. When you're bored, the brain goes into default mode network. It's not only healthy for you, but it may also shape the very essence of your identity.

item.title: A radical theory says the universe is twice as old as we thought
item.description: A provocative new cosmological model suggests the Universe could be 26.7 billion years old and might not need dark matter or dark energy to explain its behavior. University of Ottawa researchers tested the theory against several major astronomical observations, finding that it could explain galaxy rotation, cosmic expansion, and the formation of early elements.

item.title: BOE Should Raise Key Rate to Around 5%, U.K. Economic Think Tank Says
item.description: Bank of England policymakers were set to move too slowly, the National Institute of Economic and Social Research said, urging them to raise the key rate to around 5% to tame inflation within three years.

item.description: Record renewable energy growth is driving climate progress in some countries, but Germany and many major emitters are falling behind.

item.title: Ukraine captures first Indonesian prisoner of war amid surge in Russian recruitment
item.description: Capture of man from Java follows reports that hundreds are being recruited from the south-east Asian country as Moscow seeks to boost its war effort Ukraine says it has captured its first Indonesian prisoner of war, amid what it says is a spike in recruitment by Russia from the south-east Asian nation. The 49-year-old man from Java was taken to Ukraine’s Zaporizhzhia region to take part in a Russian assault, but managed to reach Ukrainian-held territory after the group came under drone attack, according to Ukraine’s state-run I Want to Live project. He was then captured by the Ukrainians. Continue reading...

item.title: No Good Choices on Iran
item.description: As top Trump aides clash over a strategy to end the war, the administration is weighing escalation, narrower strikes and diplomacy.

item.title: The thermostat wars tearing couples apart: ‘It’s hard to feel sexy when you’re freezing cold’
item.description: Almost two-thirds of bedfellows disagree about the perfect room temperature – and the issue can affect office workers and housemates too. It oftens lead to subterfuge and skulduggery. So is there any way to reach a truce? Recently I read an item on Threads that made me laugh out loud. “New dating app idea: post your thermostat settings to find your match.” The poster then revealed their own preferences: a balmy 24C by day and a chilly 19C at bedtime. The suggestion elicited a rush of responses. “As someone who married outside their thermostat bracket, all I can say is that this is the most brilliant idea ever,” enthused one user. “Get outta here with that daytime terrarium,” responded another. “Are you storing pallets of produce in your house that you need to keep cold?” chimed in a third. Continue reading...

item.title: Cancer-fighting chewing gum slashes HPV levels by up to 93%
item.description: A surprising new weapon against microbes linked to head and neck cancer could be as simple as chewing gum. Scientists developed a bioengineered gum that reduced HPV levels by up to 93% in oral samples from cancer patients and nearly eliminated two harmful bacterial species after a single dose of its extract. Even more promising, the treatment spared beneficial bacteria in the mouth.

item.title: ICE Deportation Flight Carrying Iranians Turns Back and Lands in Arizona
item.description: The Iranian immigrants in the plane were scheduled to be flown to Pakistan and then transferred to Iran, lawyers for the group said.

item.title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to 40% higher odds of stroke
item.description: New research involving more than 440,000 Americans links cannabis use to increased cardiovascular risk, with occasional users showing 40% higher odds of reporting a history of stroke. The findings suggest that even infrequent marijuana use may warrant concern, although researchers have not established that cannabis directly causes strokes or heart disease.

item.description: Users visiting the Apple Support Community tonight were greeted with a message informing them that the platform will permanently shut down on November 20. Here are the details. more…

item.title: Scientists discover why some mosquitoes love you and others don't
item.description: A surprising new study reveals that mosquitoes have very different tastes in humans, with each species attracted to its own combination of skin odors, chemicals, and bacteria. The discovery challenges the idea of a universal mosquito magnet and could lead to more effective repellents against dangerous disease-spreading mosquitoes.

item.title: Scientists discover a giant 66-pound rodent that lived 34 million years ago
item.description: Scientists have uncovered fossils of a giant rodent that lived in Thailand 34 million years ago, revealing that enormous rodents evolved much earlier than previously thought. Named Yakamys sirindhornae, the ancient animal may have weighed around 66 pounds, roughly twice as much as other known rodents of its time.

item.description: Following last week’s livestream , when Labrinth composed and recorded a song overnight at Apple Tower Theatre in Los Angeles on the new touchscreen MacBook Pro , the single is now available on Apple Music. Here are the details. more…

item.title: 237-million-year-old fossils reveal a bizarre armored sea amphibian
item.description: A bizarre, heavily armored amphibian roamed the oceans 237 million years ago, despite the fact that modern amphibians cannot survive entirely in saltwater. Discovered in China, the giant salamander-sized creature may be the first known amphibian to have adapted to a fully marine existence.

item.description: Double amputee Zaher told the BBC last year about his favourite footballer and a dream of being able to walk again.

item.description: Forecasters warn that this year's El Niño could be one of the strongest on record, with heavy rain and flooding in Kenya.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03660-5 Mapping the movements of wildlife across the Amazon and other regions to their exposure to human activities can inform protection initiatives.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03637-4 The waters around the zone of floating debris appear greener and bluer on account of high levels of tiny bits of plastic.

item.title: Salty grains in Saturn’s outermost ring formed from the slow freeze of plumes from the moon Enceladus
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03489-y One of Saturn’s rings consists of a diverse population of icy and rocky grains, each with a distinct composition. How this came about might now have an explanation.

item.title: Daily briefing: Should old, bad science be culled from the literature?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03675-y AI tools that summarize scientific literature are picking up decades-old flawed papers — should they be retracted? Plus, the first image of a black hole holds up to scrutiny and how the Artemis II mission might have disrupted GPS.

item.title: Cacti are severely threatened by drought in a warming world
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03496-z Forecasts of the effects that climate change will have on biodiversity typically rely on long-term climate averages while excluding extreme events. Projections that include severe drought predict that a majority of the 993 cactus species assessed will see large losses of suitable climatic area: more than 25% of species could lose at least 80% of it by 2100.

item.title: Extraordinary materials shaped by the principles of complex networks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03272-z Network science has inspired the design of materials that spread out their deformation when a force is applied, have tunable stiffness and can control vibrational waves.

item.title: DeepMind’s ultra-powerful AI for genome mapping wows scientists
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03673-0 AlphaGenome 2 can predict the types of cell in which a DNA variant is likely to act.

item.title: Proteins that form the nuclear pore barrier move like liquids
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03428-x Nuclear pores control molecular traffic into and out of the cell nucleus. Measurements in living cells, together with molecular-dynamics simulations, show that flexible protein chains that form the selectivity barriers of nuclear pores are highly mobile, and that a sugar modification and the carrier protein importin-β help to preserve this dynamic state.

item.title: How to avoid aliens and live
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03515-z Silence is golden.

item.title: Earth’s early history told by 3.9-billion-year-old rocks from northern China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03499-w Ancient rocks in northern China reveal that by 3.95 billion years ago, surface-altered oceanic crust had been buried rapidly to depths greater than 50 kilometres and partly melted. This crust was derived from a mantle reservoir that had been left behind when the crust separated from the early mantle as early as 4.3 billion years ago.

item.title: Biotech innovations are an opportunity to limit climate change
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03621-y Agricultural biotechnology once found itself in opposition to environmental science. Now it could reduce the impact of food systems on global warming and biodiversity loss.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03183-z Cliff Kapono shares his advice on ways to navigate and grow two different careers.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03633-8 Nobel prizewinner’s accidental discovery led to new forms of materials, light-emitting diodes and solar cells.

item.title: Give biologists the space to be curious, not just better tools
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03669-w Technology is making biological studies more powerful than ever. But people are the real force behind discovery.

item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03640-9 A promising biotechnology company developed an approach that might treat a rare disease — but its sole employee didn’t do all the work.

item.title: Move over BMI: new obesity definition is better for predicting your health
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03636-5 A fresh approach considers waist circumference, rather than just weight and height, providing a more accurate classification.

item.title: New culprit in early Alzheimer’s: blood–brain barrier blocks protective proteins
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03655-2 The brain relies on crucial proteins to maintain neurons. This system is disrupted in mice with neurological disease.

item.title: AI’s energy paradox: will the AI boom strain energy systems or be the source of solutions?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03412-5 Ginelle Greene-Dewasmes is leading a community of interdisciplinary specialists exploring how to make the energy use of artificial intelligence net-positive.

item.title: Retractions of old papers are on the rise: when should bad science be culled?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03624-9 Decades-old papers are increasingly being pulled from the literature, bringing a host of challenges.

item.title: Author or just ‘acknowledged’? How women are not gaining full credit for research
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03448-7 An analysis of who is more likely to get authorship than acknowledgement highlights the influence of a researcher’s gender and status.

item.title: Engineered bacteria are weaning farms away from synthetic fertilizers
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03641-8 Scientists are editing microbes to supply more nitrogen to staple crops.

item.title: Proposed approach for diagnosing obesity outperforms old method
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03425-0 A framework for diagnosing obesity that was proposed in 2025 incorporates waist circumference and related measures and distinguishes clinical from preclinical obesity on the basis of obesity-induced organ dysfunction. In an international multi-cohort study of 844,108 adults, this framework outperformed conventional body-mass-index-based criteria in diagnosing obesity and stratifying mortality risk.

item.title: Personal incentives for public officials drove a drop in China’s fertility
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03274-x Once the promotion prospects of bureaucrats became tied to birth targets, the country’s one-child policy became more effective. Can the state now reverse this effect?

item.title: Can green technologies deliver energy security in an unstable world?
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03409-0 As global energy markets grapple with a period of sustained political volatility, researchers are digging deep for solutions.

item.title: Human replisomes direct a dedicated leading-strand primase for fork restart
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11204-0 Structural and biochemical studies show that the CMG helicase directly recruits PRIMPOL for leading-strand repriming, enabling replication fork restart and limiting post-replicative DNA gaps.

item.title: Bureaucratic incentives shaped effectiveness of the one-child policy in China
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11232-w Stronger bureaucratic incentives under China’s one vote veto policy intensified enforcement of the one-child policy, accounting for nearly half of China’s fertility decline during the 1990s.

item.title: Validation of clinical and preclinical obesity across global cohorts
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11237-5 A large-scale data analysis assesses the Lancet Commission’s proposed diagnostic framework for obesity, finding that this framework, in which BMI is combined with other criteria, such as waist circumference and organ function, is more useful than classifications based on BMI alone.

item.title: UNC13A splice correction rescues synaptic dysfunction induced by TDP-43 loss
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11256-2 TDP-43 loss induces a predegenerative state in which neurons remain structurally intact and suffer a substantial breakdown in synaptic communication; a therapeutic strategy is found that corrects UNC13A cryptic splicing by using splice-switching antisense oligonucleotides.

item.title: NRF2 is a mechanosensitive checkpoint for NLRP3 inflammasome activation
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11324-7 The stiffness of the extracellular matrix is identified as a pivotal factor that influences activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in vitro and in vivo.

item.title: Non-halogen aqueous electrolytes for four-electron iodine conversion
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11282-0 An electrolyte framework that harnesses anionic chemistry to coordinate the interfacial microenvironment and molecular interactions enables reversible four-electron iodine conversion in halogen-free aqueous electrolytes, and is validated in metal–iodine batteries.

item.title: Bistable regulation of adipocyte heterogeneity governs thermogenesis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11308-7 IL-1β from neutrophils and macrophages stabilizes nearby brown adipocytes in a low-UCP1 state; cold temperature reduces IL-1β via sympathetic nerves, leading to transition to a high-UCP1 state and increased thermogenesis, while higher temperatures have the opposite effect.

item.title: Epigenetic heterogeneity in breast tumours informs diagnosis and prognosis
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11230-y Single-cell epigenetic analyses reveal a conserved epigenetic signature across patients that may help identify those at increased risk for disease relapse in breast cancer.

item.title: A plant RNA-binding protein senses 2′,3′-cNMP produced by insect effectors
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11259-z The rice RNA-binding protein NIB1 detects 2′,3′-cyclic nucleotide products from insect saliva RNase, forming nuclear condensates that recruit EDS1 to activate defence, revealing a conserved messenger-based immune pathway in plants.

item.title: Flexible rubber blades for tidal turbines
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11278-w Flexible tidal turbine blades with passive trailing-edge deformation match the energy yield of active pitch-controlled blades while reducing fatigue-inducing load fluctuations by up to one-third, lowering maintenance complexity.

item.title: Hadean mantle depletion and 3.95-Gyr subduction implied by North China rocks
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11280-2 Analysis of a 3.95-Gyr-old trondhjemitic gneiss from eastern Hebei, China, reveals a composition suggesting a low-temperature altered basaltic source, that originated from a mantle depleted in the Hadean, was most likely transported to mantle depths through a transient subduction event and partially melted to produce the trondhjemite.

item.title: Human land use drives microplastic abundance in terrestrial wildlife
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11285-x Microplastic burdens in Brazilian tapirs and anteaters rise with human-modified land use and proximity to development, however animals in remote habitats also carry microplastics, showing that landscape change and individual space use jointly shape wildlife exposure.

item.title: Transient nuclear softening for zygotic gene activation in mice
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11240-w A distinct physical nuclear state acquired by embryos at the beginning of life supports the initiation of the zygotic transcription program.

item.title: Suppression of epithelial proliferation and tumorigenesis by IgA
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11264-2 Experiments in mouse models show that immunoglobulin A in the gut lumen has a role in regulating the turnover of colon epithelial cells and reduces the susceptibility of mice to colorectal cancer.

item.title: Evolutionary dynamics in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11269-x The somatic evolutionary histories of haematopoietic cells in the years preceding acute myeloid leukaemia diagnosis show that the clonal dynamics of blood comply with a set of simple evolutionary rules.

item.title: Scale-rich network-based metamaterials
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11191-2 A network-science-based framework that embeds network heterogeneity into mechanical metamaterials is used to produce scale-rich metamaterials that exhibit properties inaccessible to traditional single-scale systems.

item.title: The molecular basis of replication fork restart via repriming by PRIMPOL
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11276-y PRIMPOL is recruited to stalled forks through an interaction with the replicative helicase CDC45–MCM2–7–GINS, facilitating primer handover from PRIMPOL to the high-fidelity polymerase ε, minimizing mutagenic DNA synthesis.

item.title: Domain-alteration chimeras rewire oncogenic complexes in prostate cancer
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11262-4 A novel therapeutic modality enforces non-native androgen receptor (AR)–p300/CBP interactions to collapse AR transcriptional programs, producing super-inhibitory, lineage-selective suppression of metastatic prostate cancer and establishing domain-alteration chimeras as a broadly applicable therapeutic strategy leveraging induced proximity.

item.title: Glycosylation and importins liquefy the FG barrier in live nuclear pores
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11258-0 Nuclear pore proteins maintain a fluid, spatially organized barrier through coordinated molecular interactions, explaining how cells achieve selective transport and reconciling competing models of pore structure.

item.title: Severe drought and warming increase the extinction risk of cacti
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11265-1 Severe drought and warming will substantially increase the loss of suitable climatic area for cactus species.

item.title: Low-power 2D CFETs using single-crystal high-κ dielectrics
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11272-2 A transferable single-crystal anatase titanium dioxide dielectric enables high-quality interfaces with two-dimensional semiconductors, yielding near-ideal switching, low hysteresis and ultra-low-power complementary transistors and inverters.

item.title: Independent interferometric observable confirms black hole shadow in M87*
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11241-9 An imaging algorithm using closure-invariant formalism and diffusion-based reconstruction applied to supermassive black hole very long baseline radio interferometry datasets enables independent recovery of the ring-like shadow and mass that is free from the usual calibration and imaging assumptions.

item.title: Mitochondrial protein import defects enhance tumour immunogenicity
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11249-1 Inhibition of mitochondrial protein import can enhance tumour immunogenicity by promoting mitochondrial DNA release.

item.title: Metasurface waveguides for all-day augmented reality glasses
item.description: Nature, Published online: 11 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11277-x An all-day-wearable augmented reality glasses prototype using a dual-layer metasurface-based waveguide and three matched grating patterns achieves a 30° field of view in an 8 × 8-mm2 two-dimensional eyebox while maintaining high luminance efficiency.

item.title: Astronomers discover hidden alien planet in James Webb images
item.description: A breakthrough in telescope imaging could reveal countless alien worlds that have been hiding in plain sight. Scientists developed a new technique that uses a digital twin of the James Webb Space Telescope to remove the overwhelming glare of stars, making faint exoplanets two to 15 times easier to detect than with conventional methods. The technology has already uncovered a previously hidden planet in existing telescope data and could reveal many more.

item.title: The laundry miracle: how to solve 10 stubborn problems – from stains to rough towels to ‘permastank’
item.description: For 1 million people on Reddit, the science of clothes-washing is a regular topic of discussion. I tried out their tips and discovered some simple, sustainable answers It started with a sunscreen stain – a yellowed collar on a white T-shirt that persisted wash after wash. A spray of stain remover did nothing; drying the shirt in the sun made it worse. An internet rabbit hole took me to the r/laundry subreddit , where I found my people: 995,000 of them, nerding out over the chemistry of clothes-washing. “People want to take better care of their stuff, but don’t have the knowledge,” says Eric Thompson, a former management consultant based near Seattle who moderates the forum under the name KismaiAesthetics. He took on the mantle after seeing someone suggest white vinegar to treat a burrito stain on an anorak. “If you pour vinegar on a burrito grease stain on white nylon, you now have orange nylon for eternity,” he says. “Acids bind colour to dye sites on nylon.” Continue reading...

item.title: Alzheimer’s may have early warning signs outside the brain
item.description: A surprising discovery suggests that some early signs of Alzheimer’s disease may begin outside the brain. Using miniature laboratory systems made from human cells, scientists found that genetic mutations associated with inherited Alzheimer’s can disrupt nerve-to-muscle connections without any involvement from the brain or spinal cord. This could help explain why some patients experience changes in balance, walking, and coordination long before memory problems develop.

item.title: Manchester City’s weaknesses under Enzo Maresca are being exposed
item.description: After three straight defeats, City’s manager says he will use the international break to reassess. Their problems may go beyond tactics Sign up for our free newsletter here Enzo Maresca seemed, if not quite baffled by his side’s Saturday defeat to Nottingham Forest, then at least a little put out. After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. The three defeats were all different, Maresca said, although in all of them City had had more possession and more chances. In the 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa two weeks ago, City had 63% of the ball and had 15 chances to Villa’s eight. item.title: Scientists discover a surprising link between acorns and lyme disease
item.description: After more than 35 years of research, scientists have uncovered surprising clues about what really drives Lyme disease risk. Contrary to longstanding assumptions, deer populations appear less important than mice, which can fuel a 40% increase in tick numbers the following year. Even acorn production can predict tick population surges two years in advance, while extreme temperatures may be far less deadly to ticks than scientists once believed.

item.title: Crime pays: how Grand Theft Auto became a cultural colossus
item.description: Ever since it crashed on to PC and consoles in the late 90s, GTA has been tearing up the game-making rulebook. We explore how its cultural references, rebel spirit and sprawling sense of freedom make it a definitive work of art In the 00s, when the Grand Theft Auto developer Rockstar Games revealed a new project, video game writers from all over the UK would make the journey to the company’s office in London. They would be ushered one by one into a darkened room to sit facing an enormous TV. There would be a dish of sweets on a low bench in front of them but, in the reverential hush that descended, it was never entirely clear if it was acceptable to eat them. After a few moments, the screen would come to life. Rockstar would sometimes begin its presentation not with footage from its new game, but clips from classic movies. This is the context of what we are making, Rockstar was saying, and that is where we belong. Continue reading...

item.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
item.description: Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. Jonathan Wilson Match report: Nottingham Forest 3

item.title: Scientists discover a hidden warning sign of cannabis addiction

item.description: Swindon manager has a history of viral outbursts but fans want a united club and manager they can support In Ian Holloway’s often madcap managerial orbit, this was simply the latest in a steady succession of eccentric outbursts. Eyes bulging as he spoke, he boomed the letter “D” and promptly stabbed himself in the chest with an imaginary dagger. Next came the letter “M” alongside a blow from another invisible knife. Finally, a “W” followed by a jab to the heart. “Dead. Man. Walking,” he declared, pausing for effect between words and briefly falling into an Oscar-worthy zombie stupor. “That’s how it feels.” To an offbeat press conference genre containing seagulls following trawlers and self-proclaimed special ones, it was a crazy new entry worthy of its subsequent viral nature. item.title: Transfer window verdict: how every Premier League club fared
item.description: The British transfer record was equalled and one club signed no fewer than 18 players in another hectic summer Bringing in Christos Tzolis, Bruno Guimarães and Ezri Konsa was a strong start to the window but could Arsenal’s failure to sign a marquee attacker cost them in the long run? They began targeting Morgan Rogers before pivoting to Vinícius Júnior when the England forward went to Chelsea, only to end up disappointed when Vinícius signed a new deal with Real Madrid. Julián Alvarez made clear he had no intention of joining from Atlético Madrid in the final days of the window and Arsenal kept their powder dry despite sanctioning the exits of Gabriel Jesus to Barcelona and Ethan Nwaneri to Borussia Dortmund. Should Gabriel Martinelli complete his move to Al-Hilal as expected in the coming days – the Saudi Pro League window remains open – a few injuries could leave Arteta short. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...

item.title: Aitana Bonmatí makes Guardian top 100 history with third title in a row
item.description: The margin may have got smaller but the brilliant Spanish midfielder makes it a hat-trick of No 1 finishes They say the best things come in threes, and Aitana Bonmatí has written herself into the Guardian’s top 100 history as the first player to finish at the top of the tree for a third consecutive year. Last year the majestic midfielder emulated her Barcelona and Spain teammate Alexia Putellas by winning for a second year running , but the 27-year-old has now gone one better, establishing herself once again at the top of the women’s game.
